The FDA's adverse event database holds 20.7 million spontaneous reports, and
regulators screen them with disproportionality statistics. This milestone pushes
a single partition — 12,000 reports — through every layer of the pipeline, to
find out what breaks first.

## 12,000 reports rebuilt byte for byte

The partition arrives as 807 MB of JSON and leaves as 4.6 MB of Parquet, 175×
smaller, with every field kept. That nothing was lost is not an assertion: the
tables are read back, the nested source document is reconstructed from them, and
all 12,000 come back byte-identical.

The test that proves it was itself checked. An earlier version stripped nulls
from both documents before comparing, which would have hidden any real
difference behind a passing count. The source carries zero explicit nulls —
measured, every value at every depth — so the comparison is one-sided and means
what it says.

## The ranking is arithmetically right and clinically absurd

PRR over a 2×2 of distinct reports, artifact terms excluded, three co-reports
minimum. The first row is nail fungus on a buprenorphine patch. Recomputed by
hand: a = 9, b = 9, c = 1, d = 11,981, summing to exactly 12,000. The query is
correct and the answer is nonsense.

The screening criterion does not rescue it. Evans keeps 85% of pairs, and every
implausible one clears it comfortably — χ² is *large* precisely because the
expected count is 0.015. No threshold separates a duplicate from a signal.

**Limitations.** One partition. No entity resolution, so `INFLIXIMAB` and
`REMICADE` are different drugs. No deduplication. Three co-reports minimum.
Disproportionate reporting is not causation.

## 1% of the reports manufacture two thirds of the pairs

A report naming 90 drugs and 10 events asserts 900 drug–event pairs. This
partition's median report names two, and its 99th percentile names 27. The 125
reports above that line supply the evidence for 18,946 of the 28,540 pairs.

```{python}
#| label: fig-crowding
#| fig-cap: "Every drug–event pair reaching three co-reports, against how many drugs the reports behind it name. The ratio climbs with the width of the document."
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "the plotting code"

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas
import seaborn


seaborn.set_theme(style="darkgrid")

pairs = pandas.read_csv("data/prr_top.csv", comment="#")

ordinary = pairs[pairs.crowded == 0]
crowded = pairs[pairs.crowded == 1]


figure, axes = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.4, 5.2))

axes.scatter(ordinary.crowding, ordinary.prr,
             s=7, alpha=0.25, linewidths=0, color="#0072B2")

axes.scatter(crowded.crowding, crowded.prr,
             s=7, alpha=0.25, linewidths=0, color="#D55E00")

axes.axvline(27, color="#3C3C3C", linewidth=1.1, linestyle=(0, (5, 4)))


axes.text(24, 2.2e4, "99th percentile", color="#3C3C3C", fontsize=9, ha="right")

axes.text(3.2, 3.5e3, f"{len(ordinary):,} pairs\nfrom ordinary reports",
          color="#0072B2", fontsize=10.5)

axes.text(30, 0.22, f"{len(crowded):,} pairs\nfrom 125 reports",
          color="#D55E00", fontsize=10.5)


axes.set_xscale("log")
axes.set_yscale("log")
axes.set_xlim(0.9, 130)
axes.set_ylim(0.08, 4e4)
axes.set_xlabel("distinct drugs named by the reports behind the pair")
axes.set_ylabel("proportional reporting ratio")

plt.show()
```

Nine of those 125 are one case. All Canadian, all serious, filed within three
months by six different manufacturers, drug lists overlapping at a Jaccard
median of 0.48 — and two of them share a company number and an identical
ten-term reaction list.

Remove the crowded pairs and the top of the table changes character: risperidone
and gynaecomastia, a documented prolactin effect. One pair is not a finding. It
is the first sign that the method works once the input is clean, and cleaning
the input is the next milestone.
